subject: Archaeology
title: The Antikythera Mechanism: Ancient Computer
description: A tiny lesson with a big payoff: The Antikythera Mechanism: Ancient Computer.

hook.text: A corroded lump from a Roman shipwreck turned out to be the most complex mechanism built by the ancient world.

buildup.text: Found in 1901 off Antikythera, Greece, the device had over 30 interlocking bronze gears hidden inside a wooden box.

discovery.text: It predicted eclipses, tracked the Moon's irregular orbit, and even calculated the dates of the Olympic Games.

twist.text: Nothing remotely this complex was made again until European clockmakers in the 1300s.

climax.text: CT scans in 2006 revealed tiny inscriptions — an instruction manual.

punchline.text: Greeks built an analog computer 2,000 years ago.

quiz.question: What is most astonishing about the Antikythera Mechanism?
options: It was powered by steam, predating the Industrial Revolution
Nothing this complex was built again until European clockmakers 1,400 years later
It was found intact and in perfect working condition

details.summary: The Antikythera Mechanism is a 2,000-year-old Greek device with interlocking bronze gears that predicted astronomical events, eclipses, and Olympic game dates. Found in a shipwreck in 1901, it demonstrates technology thought impossible for the ancient world.
details.whyItMatters: The Antikythera Mechanism proves ancient Greeks achieved mechanical sophistication not seen again for over a thousand years. It forces reconsideration of ancient technological capabilities and challenges progress narratives.
takeaways: A 2,000-year-old mechanical computer with bronze gears
Predicted eclipses, planetary positions, and Olympic dates
Technology this complex didn't reappear for over 1,000 years

faq.question: What could the Antikythera Mechanism calculate?
faq.answer: It tracked the Sun, Moon, and five known planets through the zodiac, predicted solar and lunar eclipses using the Saros cycle, and calculated the timing of pan-Hellenic athletic games. Its gear train of at least 30 bronze gears encoded centuries of astronomical knowledge.

faq.question: Why was this technology lost for so long?
faq.answer: The Roman conquest of Greece disrupted Greek scientific traditions. Knowledge of precision gear-making may have been held by a small group of specialists. Without institutional support to train successors, the technology died with its practitioners and was not reinvented for centuries.
